title: Gravitational Potential and Potential Energy

notes: **Gravitational potential V:** the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to a point, without acceleration. For a point mass M: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$. At infinity $V = 0$, and everywhere else V is negative because gravity does positive work as the mass approaches — the field does the work, so potential decreases.

**Escape and binding — the negative-energy picture**

| Situation | Total energy | Bound? |
|---|---|---|
| Body at rest at infinity | 0 | marginally free |
| Satellite in circular orbit | $-GMm/2r$ < 0 | bound |
| Body at escape speed | 0 | just escapes |
| Body slower than escape speed | < 0 | falls back |
| Energy to escape from orbit r | $+GMm/2r$ must be added | — |

### Deep dive: why gravitational potential is negative

Potential is defined *relative to infinity*, where it is taken as zero. Since gravity attracts, bringing a unit mass from infinity toward a mass M means the field does positive work on it — so the stored (potential) energy must fall below zero: $V = -GM/r$. The negative sign is not a convention quirk; it encodes that a bound system has less energy than a free one, and that energy $+GMm/r$ must be *supplied* to escape (the escape-energy idea). Potential energy of a pair is $U = -GMm/r$, and near the surface this reduces to the familiar $mgh$ because $GM/r^2 = g$ there. NEB loves asking for the *total* energy of an orbiting satellite: $E = -GMm/2r$, half the potential energy.

```svg Potential well — V = -GM/r deepens toward the mass
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 280" font-family="Segoe UI" font-size="13"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="280" fill="#ffffff"/><path d="M60 80 C 180 80, 220 240, 320 240 C 420 240, 460 80, 580 80" fill="none" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="2.5"/><circle cx="320" cy="240" r="12" fill="#991b1b"/><text x="320" y="265" text-anchor="middle" fill="#991b1b">mass M</text><text x="110" y="65" fill="#374151">V = 0 at infinity</text><text x="320" y="225" text-anchor="middle" fill="#166534">V = −GM/r (deepest at surface)</text><text x="320" y="40" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6b7280">potential well: energy +GMm/r needed to climb out</text></svg>
```

**Gravitational potential energy U:** the work done against gravity in assembling a system; for two masses separated by r: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. It is the energy of the whole system, not of one mass alone. U is negative because the system is bound — you must supply $GMm/r$ of energy to separate the masses to infinity.

**Why the minus sign matters:** potential energy is defined with zero at infinity. Since the force is attractive, energy is released (and PE decreases) as masses come together. A satellite in orbit at radius r has $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — its total mechanical energy is $E = K + U = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, which is negative, confirming a bound orbit.

**Near Earth's surface:** for small heights h above the surface, $U = mgh$. This is the constant-g approximation of $-\frac{GMm}{r}$: since $\Delta(1/r) \approx -h/R^2$, the change matches $mgh$. Use $mgh$ only for $h \ll R$; use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for large altitudes (satellites, rockets).

**Worked example — escape energy:** to launch a mass m from Earth's surface (R) to infinity you must supply $GMm/R$. Numerically for m = 1 kg: $\frac{6.67\times 10^{-11}\times 5.97\times 10^{24}}{6.37\times 10^6} \approx 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 62.5 \text{ MJ}$ per kg. This energy corresponds to the escape speed 11.2 km/s.

**Potential vs potential energy vs field:** field $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ (the force per unit mass, a vector); potential V is a scalar (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$. The field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ radially.

**Equipotential surfaces:** surfaces of constant V. Moving along an equipotential surface requires zero work; the field is always perpendicular to these surfaces. For a point mass, equipotentials are concentric spheres.

**Superposition:** for multiple masses, $V = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i}{r_i}\right)$ and $U = \sum\left(-\frac{GM_i m}{r_i}\right)$ — potentials add as scalars, which is much simpler than adding force vectors.

```svg Equipotential spheres — concentric around the mass
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 280" font-family="Segoe UI" font-size="13"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="280" fill="#ffffff"/><g fill="none" stroke-width="2"><circle cx="320" cy="140" r="30" stroke="#991b1b"/><circle cx="320" cy="140" r="60" stroke="#a16207"/><circle cx="320" cy="140" r="95" stroke="#166534"/><circle cx="320" cy="140" r="130" stroke="#1d4ed8"/></g><circle cx="320" cy="140" r="8" fill="#111827"/><text x="320" y="180" text-anchor="middle" fill="#374151">closer sphere = more negative V</text><text x="320" y="270" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6b7280" font-size="12">no work is done moving a mass along an equipotential surface</text></svg>
```
confusion: ❌ 'Potential and potential energy are the same.' ✅ Potential V is work per unit mass (J/kg); potential energy $U = mV$ (J). V belongs to a point in the field; U belongs to the mass–field system.
❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ '$U = mgh$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: $mgh$ is the CHANGE in $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface ($-\frac{GM}{R}$) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes $-\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but $U \approx 0$). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

universalFacts: Gravitational potential energy is exactly the 'missing' energy that binds systems — this is why the binding energy of Earth + satellite equals $|U|$.

❌ 'Negative energy is unphysical.' ✅ Negative potential energy simply means the system is BOUND — energy must be added to separate it. It is a matter of the reference at infinity.
❌ '$U = mgh$ and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ disagree.' ✅ They agree for small heights: $mgh$ is the CHANGE in $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ near the surface. Use the right one for the régime.
❌ 'Potential is maximum at Earth's surface.' ✅ Potential is most negative at the surface ($-\frac{GM}{R}$) and rises toward zero with altitude — at infinity it reaches the (higher) value 0.
❌ 'Doubling the distance doubles the potential energy.' ✅ $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ — doubling r halves the magnitude, so U becomes $-\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (less negative).

❌ 'A satellite far away has lots of potential energy.' ✅ A far-away satellite has potential energy near ZERO (least negative, but $U \approx 0$). It needs enormous kinetic energy (orbital speed) that comes from the launch energy.

universalFacts: Gravitational potential energy is exactly the 'missing' energy that binds systems — this is why the binding energy of Earth + satellite equals $|U|$.
The concept of potential is useful because it is scalar: complex many-body problems reduce to addition rather than vector resolution.
Near a black hole, gravitational potential becomes so deep ($-\frac{GM}{r}$) that even light cannot escape — the origin of the event horizon.
Gravitational potential determines whether planets retain atmospheres: gas molecules with thermal speeds above the local escape speed leak away.
The Voyager probes were launched using the escape-energy budget — their final trajectory traced the potential wells of the Sun and giant planets.
examples: U of 1000 kg satellite at $r = 6.8\times 10^{6} \text{ m}$: $U = -\frac{GMm}{r} = -5.9\times 10^{10} \text{ J}$.
Escape energy per kg: $GM/R = 6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J} \approx 17 \text{ kWh}$ per kg.
Near surface: a 2 kg mass lifted 10 m gains $U = mgh = 196 \text{ J}$.
Total energy of circular orbit: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ — negative, so the orbit is bound.

keyPoints: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ is negative, approaching zero at infinity.
$U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ is the energy of the (bound) system, negative for attraction.
Near Earth's surface $U = mgh$ is the appropriate approximation.
Total energy of a circular orbit is negative: $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$.
specialNotes: Both V and U are defined with reference zero at infinity — that is why they are negative.
Use $U = mgh$ only for small heights ($h \ll R$); use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$ for space-scale problems.
Potential is a scalar — use scalar addition with multiple masses.
The escape energy equals $|U|$ at the surface: $GMm/R$.
NEB may ask 'derive $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ starting from $F = \frac{GMm}{r^2}$' — know the integration step.
importantStatements: Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$.
Gravitational potential energy of two masses is $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$, taking zero at infinity.
For small heights near Earth's surface, $U = mgh$.
The gravitational field is the negative gradient of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$.
A satellite in a circular orbit has total energy $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$ (bound system).
importantNotes: $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ (potential) and $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ (potential energy) both take zero at infinity — hence negative for attracted masses.
Near Earth's surface use $U = mgh$; for space-scale distances use the inverse-r form.
The field is the negative slope of the potential: $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$.
Binding energy of a two-mass system $= |U| = GMm/r$.
Total energy of a circular orbit ($E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$) is negative — a signature of a bound state.
examShortTricks: Escape-energy shortcut: energy to infinity = $GMm/R = mgR$ (since $g = \frac{GM}{R^2}$).
V at surface $\approx -6.25\times 10^{7} \text{ J/kg}$ for Earth — compare planets by this value.
When moving closer to a mass, U becomes MORE negative (energy is released).
Use $mgh$ only when the height is small compared with Earth's radius — a quick sanity check.
examNotes: Derivation of $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ from integrating $F = \frac{GMm}{r^2}$ is a standard question.
Numericals on satellite total energy and escape energy are frequently asked.
Conceptual MCQ: why is potential energy negative? → because zero is at infinity and gravity is attractive.
Linking $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ to a $V$–$r$ graph slope appears in higher-level questions.

importantConcepts: Gravitational potential $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ is scalar work per unit mass.
Gravitational potential energy $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ equals the negative binding energy.
Near the surface $U = mgh$; far away use $-\frac{GMm}{r}$.
$g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$ links the vector field to the scalar potential.

summary: Gravitational potential $V = -\frac{GM}{r}$ is the work per unit mass to bring a test mass from infinity; potential energy $U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ is the negative binding energy of two masses. Near the surface $U \approx mgh$. The field relates to the potential by $g = -\frac{dV}{dr}$, and circular orbits have total energy $E = -\frac{GMm}{2r}$, confirming their bound nature.

subtopics.name: Potential energy
points: U = -GMm/r, with zero defined at infinity
Negative because gravity is attractive and work must be done to separate the masses
Near the surface this reduces to U = mgh

subtopics.name: Potential
points: V = U/m = -GM/r, the work per unit mass to bring a unit mass from infinity
Potential is a scalar, so it adds algebraically with no vector work

subtopics.name: Relation to field
points: g = -dV/dr — field strength is the negative potential gradient
Potential decreases toward the mass; field points in the direction of decreasing potential
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines

subtopics.name: Work done
points: Work done moving a mass between two points equals m times the potential difference
Work done along an equipotential is zero
Work done depends only on endpoints, not the path — gravity is conservative

subtopics.name: Escape and binding
points: Total energy zero means the body just escapes
Binding energy is the energy needed to remove a mass to infinity
For a satellite, total energy is -GMm/2r and binding energy is +GMm/2r

subtopics.name: Standard traps
points: Potential at the centre of a uniform sphere is finite, not infinite
Potential inside a shell is constant and equals its surface value
Do not confuse potential (J/kg) with potential energy (J)
